nodes.label: Decentralisation
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Transfer of power from central and state governments to local governments. Constitutionalised in India by 73rd and 74th Amendments (1992). Created three-tier panchayati raj (village, block, district) and urban local bodies (municipalities, corporations).

nodes.label: Panchayati Raj System
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Three-tier local government in rural areas: Gram Panchayat (village), Panchayat Samiti/Block Samiti (block level), Zila Parishad (district level). Gram Sabha (village assembly of all voters) supervises the Gram Panchayat. Members directly elected. Handles local development and welfare.

nodes.label: Municipalities and Municipal Corporations
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Urban local bodies for towns and cities. Municipalities for smaller towns, Municipal Corporations for big cities headed by Mayor. Members (councillors/corporators) elected. Handle urban planning, water supply, roads, sanitation, and other civic services.

nodes.label: Caste vs Race
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Caste is a social division based on birth and occupation (primarily Indian), while race is a classification based on physical features like skin colour. At the 2001 UN Conference Against Racism in Durban, Dalit groups demanded inclusion of caste discrimination on the agenda.

nodes.label: Patriarchy
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: System that values men more and gives them power over women. Manifested in India through lower female literacy (54% vs 76% for men), declining child sex ratio due to sex-selective abortion, lower wages, and dowry-related violence. Constitutional equality has not eliminated social patriarchy.

nodes.label: Declining Child Sex Ratio
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Number of girl children per 1000 boys has been declining due to sex-selective abortion (preference for male child). Lowest in Punjab, Haryana, Gujarat, Himachal Pradesh. Despite Pre-Natal Diagnostic Techniques Act, practice continues in many regions.

nodes.label: Popular Struggles in Democracy
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Democracy evolves through popular struggles, not just consensus. Defining moments involve conflict between those exercising power and those aspiring for it. Struggles happen during transition to democracy, expansion of democracy, or deepening of democracy.

nodes.label: Pressure Groups
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Organisations that attempt to influence government policies without directly contesting elections. Two types: sectional interest groups (trade unions, business associations) representing specific sections, and public interest groups (BAMCEF, Narmada Bachao Andolan) promoting general public interests.

nodes.label: Movement Groups
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Loose organisations attempting to influence politics through mass mobilisation rather than elections. More informal and flexible than interest groups. Examples: Narmada Bachao Andolan, Right to Information movement, anti-liquor movement, women's movement, environmental movement.

nodes.label: Sectional Interest Groups
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Groups representing specific sections of society: trade unions for workers, business associations for employers, professional bodies for lawyers/doctors/teachers. Seek to promote interests of their particular section. Their principal concern is betterment of their members.

nodes.label: Public Interest Groups
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Groups that aim to help groups other than their own members. Also called promotional or advocacy groups. Examples: BAMCEF (Backward and Minority Communities Employees Federation) fights for Dalit rights. Environmental groups work for public benefit, not just their members.

nodes.label: Relationship between Parties and Movements
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Some pressure groups are extensions of political parties (trade unions of CPI-M, BJP affiliates). Some movements develop into parties. Some maintain autonomy but engage with parties on specific issues. Both direct participation and indirect influence are valid democratic channels.

nodes.label: Direct vs Indirect Political Participation
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Direct: forming parties, contesting elections, forming governments. Indirect: pressure groups, movements, protests, demonstrations, strikes. Both are necessary channels of democratic participation. Indirect participation especially important for citizens who cannot directly enter politics.

nodes.label: Influence of Pressure Groups on Politics
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Pressure groups influence in many ways: information campaigns, organising protests, business groups funding parties. Their influence can be positive (deepening democracy) or negative (small groups gaining disproportionate power through money/connections). Healthy democracy needs both parties and pressure groups.

nodes.label: Political Party
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: A group of people who come together to contest elections and hold power. Agree on policies and programmes for collective good. Three components: leaders, active members, followers. Reflect fundamental political divisions. A necessary condition for democracy.

nodes.label: Functions of Political Parties
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Seven functions: (1) contest elections, (2) put forward policies, (3) make laws in legislature, (4) form and run governments, (5) role of opposition, (6) shape public opinion, (7) provide access to government machinery. Parties are essential because without them, no accountability for how the country is run.

nodes.label: One-Party System
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Only one party allowed to control government. China is an example. Not considered democratic because it does not allow free competition. Some countries have one dominant party even with multi-party system (like PRI in Mexico until 2000).

nodes.label: Two-Party System
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Power usually changes between two main parties. Others exist but rarely form government. USA (Democrats and Republicans) and UK (Labour and Conservative) are examples. Provides clear choice to voters and stable governments.

nodes.label: Multi-Party System
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Several parties compete for power. More than two have reasonable chance. India is an example. Often leads to coalition governments. Allows variety of interests to enjoy representation. Can appear messy but reflects social diversity.

nodes.label: National Parties
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Parties recognised across several states with presence throughout the country. In 2006: INC, BJP, BSP, CPI, CPI(M), NCP. Must secure 6% votes in 4 states or win 2% Lok Sabha seats from 3 states. Election Commission grants recognition and allots symbols.

nodes.label: Role of Opposition Parties
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Parties that lose elections voice different views, criticise government failures, and mobilise opposition. Essential for democracy as they provide checks on ruling party. Opposition Leader in Lok Sabha has status equivalent to cabinet minister.

nodes.label: Election Commission Party Recognition
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Election Commission registers parties, grants recognition based on poll performance, and allots election symbols. Recognised parties get reserved symbols, time on state TV/radio during elections, and access to electoral rolls. Unrecognised parties must get their own symbols.

nodes.label: Partisanship
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Strong commitment to a party, group, or faction. Marked by tendency to take sides. Parties are inherently partisan as they represent a part of society. Democracy channels partisanship into competitive electoral politics.

nodes.label: Expected Outcomes of Democracy
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Democracy is expected to produce accountable, responsive government. Promotes equality, enhances dignity, improves decision-making quality, resolves conflicts peacefully, and allows correction of mistakes. Not guaranteed to deliver all socioeconomic outcomes but creates conditions for them.

nodes.label: Accountable and Responsive Government
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Most basic outcome of democracy. Government must be accountable to citizens and responsive to their needs. Ensured through regular elections, public debate, and citizens' right to information. Democracies perform better than non-democracies on this measure.

nodes.label: Transparency in Democracy
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Democracy ensures decision-making is based on norms and procedures that citizens can examine. Right to know if decisions were taken through correct procedures. Often missing in non-democratic governments. Key factor in making government accountable.

nodes.label: Democracy and Inequality
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Democracies have not been successful in reducing economic inequality. Income inequality is growing in most democratic countries. The richest 1% own disproportionate wealth. Democracy provides political equality but economic equality remains a challenge.

nodes.label: Conflict Resolution in Democracy
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Democratic governments are better at handling social differences, divisions, and conflicts. They develop procedures and institutions to negotiate differences. No permanent winner or loser. In diverse countries like India, democracy keeps unity despite diversity.

nodes.label: Legitimate Government
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Democracy produces governments that are legitimate - based on free and fair elections, acceptable to people. Even flawed democracies enjoy more legitimacy than non-democracies. People worldwide believe democracy is best form of government even when dissatisfied with current government.

nodes.label: Democratic Dissatisfaction
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Citizens are often dissatisfied with democracy in practice while supporting it in principle. This dissatisfaction is healthy - it reflects high expectations and alerts to need for improvement. People who complain about democracy are actually its greatest supporters.

nodes.label: Majority-Minority Relations in Democracy
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Democracy expected to accommodate social diversity and protect minority rights. Majority rule through elections does not mean majority community's dominance. Constitutional protections and institutional safeguards necessary for protecting minority interests.

nodes.label: Democracy as Form Not Goal
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Democracy is just a form of government that creates conditions for achieving goals. Citizens must take advantage of those conditions. Democracy cannot solve all problems but ensures a framework of equality, dignity, and accountability within which people can work towards solutions.

nodes.label: Economic Outcomes of Democracy
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Democracy's economic record is mixed. Not necessarily faster economic development than dictatorships. But provides stable economic environment, rule of law, property rights, and contractual enforcement. Less likely to face famines (as Amartya Sen argued).

nodes.label: Citizen Participation in Democracy
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Democracy provides channels for citizen participation beyond elections: public debates, pressure groups, movements, RTI. Citizens should be able to participate in decisions that affect them. Participation strengthens democracy and makes government more responsive.

nodes.label: Challenge of Civilian Control over Military
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: In many countries, military exercises control over government even after formal transition to democracy. Pakistan, Myanmar are examples. Establishing civilian supremacy over military is a key foundational challenge for many countries.

nodes.label: Challenge of Corruption in Democracy
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Corruption undermines democratic governance. Money power influences elections and policy. Citizens lose trust. RTI, independent institutions (CBI, Lokpal), judicial activism, and media scrutiny are mechanisms to combat corruption. But reducing inequality is key.

nodes.label: Reservation Policy
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Article 15(4) and 16(4) allow reservation for backward classes, SC/ST. Not a violation of equality but its fulfilment — substantive equality requires addressing existing inequalities. Supreme Court capped reservation at 50% (Indra Sawhney case 1992).

nodes.label: Right to Education
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Article 21A added by 86th Amendment 2002. Makes free and compulsory education a fundamental right for children 6-14 years. RTE Act 2009 implemented this. Moved from DPSP (Art 45) to FR.

nodes.label: Delimitation
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Process of redrawing constituency boundaries based on census data. Done by independent Delimitation Commission. Ensures roughly equal population per constituency. Last major delimitation based on 2001 census (87th Amendment froze seats till 2026 census).

nodes.label: Electronic Voting Machines (EVMs)
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Replaced paper ballots nationwide from 2004. Manufactured by BEL and ECIL. Stand-alone units (not connected to internet). VVPAT (Voter Verified Paper Audit Trail) added for verification. SC ordered VVPAT in all machines.

nodes.label: Electoral Reforms
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Ongoing reforms include: ceiling on election expenditure, state funding of elections debate, criminalisation of politics (SC ruled candidates must declare criminal cases), NOTA option introduced in 2013, right to reject debate.

nodes.label: President of India
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Head of state, elected indirectly by electoral college (MPs + elected MLAs). 5-year term. Powers include appointing PM, summoning/proroguing Parliament, ordinance-making, emergency powers. Acts on aid and advice of Council of Ministers (42nd/44th Amendments).

nodes.label: Vice President
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Ex-officio Chairman of Rajya Sabha. Elected by electoral college of both houses. Acts as President when office is vacant (max 6 months). Removed by resolution of Rajya Sabha passed by effective majority and agreed by Lok Sabha.

nodes.label: Prime Minister
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Head of government and real executive authority. Leader of majority party in Lok Sabha. Heads Council of Ministers. Advises President on appointments. Link between President and Council of Ministers. Can be removed only by losing Lok Sabha confidence.

nodes.label: Council of Ministers
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Three tiers: Cabinet Ministers, Ministers of State, Deputy Ministers. Collectively responsible to Lok Sabha (Article 75). Total size cannot exceed 15% of Lok Sabha strength (91st Amendment 2003). PM is primus inter pares.

nodes.label: Cabinet
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Inner ring of Council of Ministers. Not mentioned in Constitution (mentioned only in Article 352). Takes all important policy decisions. Functions on principle of collective responsibility — all members bound by cabinet decisions publicly.

nodes.label: Governor
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Head of state at state level. Appointed by President (not elected). 5-year term, serves at pleasure of President. Constitutional head but has discretionary powers: reserving bills for President, recommending President's Rule, appointing CM when no clear majority.

nodes.label: Chief Minister
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Head of government at state level. Leader of majority party in State Assembly. Appointed by Governor. Advises Governor on appointment of ministers. Real executive power at state level. Must retain confidence of State Assembly.

nodes.label: Presidential Election
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Indirect election by electoral college (elected MPs + elected MLAs). Single transferable vote with proportional representation. Value of votes calculated to equalize representation. Disputes decided by Supreme Court.

nodes.label: Ordinance Making Power
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: President can promulgate ordinances when Parliament not in session (Art 123). Governor can at state level (Art 213). Ordinance has same force as Act. Must be laid before legislature when it reassembles. Lapses after 6 weeks of reassembly.

nodes.label: Emergency Powers of President
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Three types: National Emergency (Art 352, war/external aggression/armed rebellion), State Emergency/President's Rule (Art 356, failure of constitutional machinery), Financial Emergency (Art 360, never used). 44th Amendment added safeguards.

nodes.label: Pardoning Power
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: President can grant pardon, reprieve, respite, remission, commutation of sentence (Art 72). Governor has similar power at state level (Art 161) but cannot pardon death sentence or court martial cases. President's power extends to all federal offences.

nodes.label: Permanent Executive (Bureaucracy)
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Civil servants who implement government policies. Recruited through UPSC. Provide continuity, expertise, and institutional memory. Include IAS, IPS, IFS and other services. Remain in office regardless of government change.

nodes.label: Parliament of India
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Supreme legislative body. Consists of President + Lok Sabha + Rajya Sabha. Makes laws, controls finances, holds executive accountable. Sovereignty of Parliament limited by Constitution (unlike British Parliament).

nodes.label: Lok Sabha (House of the People)
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Lower house, directly elected. Maximum 552 members (530 states + 20 UTs + 2 Anglo-Indians, though AI seats abolished by 104th Amendment 2020). 5-year term (can be dissolved earlier). More powerful in money matters.

nodes.label: Rajya Sabha (Council of States)
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Upper house, indirectly elected by State MLAs. Maximum 250 members (238 elected + 12 nominated by President). Permanent body — 1/3 members retire every 2 years. Cannot be dissolved. Equal power in constitutional amendments.

nodes.label: Speaker of Lok Sabha
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Presiding officer of Lok Sabha. Elected from among members. Maintains order, interprets rules, decides on disqualification under anti-defection law. Remains in office even after dissolution until new Lok Sabha meets. Casting vote only.

nodes.label: Money Bill
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Bill dealing with taxation, appropriation, borrowing. Can only be introduced in Lok Sabha. Rajya Sabha can only recommend changes within 14 days — Lok Sabha may accept or reject. Speaker certifies whether a bill is money bill (final).

nodes.label: Ordinary Bill
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Non-money bills. Can be introduced in either house. Must be passed by both houses. If disagreement, President can summon joint sitting (Art 108). Joint sitting presided by Speaker. Majority of total members present and voting decides.

nodes.label: Constitutional Amendment Bill
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Article 368: Three types. Simple majority (like ordinary law). Special majority (2/3 of members present AND voting + majority of total membership). Special majority + ratification by half the states (for federal provisions). No joint sitting.

nodes.label: Union Budget
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Annual Financial Statement presented under Article 112. Contains estimated receipts and expenditure. Charged expenditure (salaries of President, judges, etc.) not votable. Demands for grants voted by Lok Sabha. Rajya Sabha can only discuss, not vote on demands.

nodes.label: Question Hour
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: First hour of parliamentary sitting. Members ask questions to ministers. Three types: Starred (oral answer, supplementary questions allowed), Unstarred (written answer), Short notice (urgent matters). Key accountability mechanism.

nodes.label: Parliamentary Committees
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Standing committees examine bills, oversee departments. Key ones: Public Accounts Committee, Estimates Committee, Committee on Public Undertakings. PAC chaired by opposition member. Department-related standing committees cover all ministries.

nodes.label: Parliamentary Privileges
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Special rights of Parliament members. Include: freedom of speech in Parliament (no court proceedings), exemption from jury duty, freedom from arrest in civil cases during session. Breach of privilege can be punished by Parliament.

nodes.label: Joint Sitting of Parliament
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Article 108: President can summon joint sitting when houses disagree on ordinary bill. Presided by Speaker. Decision by majority. Not applicable to money bills or constitutional amendment bills. Used only 3 times so far.

nodes.label: Adjournment Motion
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Motion to draw attention to urgent matter of public importance. Only in Lok Sabha. Needs support of 50 members. Interrupts normal business. Involves censure against government. Different from calling attention motion.

nodes.label: State Legislature
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Unicameral (only Legislative Assembly) in most states. Bicameral (Assembly + Council) in 6 states: UP, Bihar, Maharashtra, Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh, Telangana. Governor is part of state legislature. MLAs directly elected.

nodes.label: Sessions: Prorogation and Dissolution
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Summoning: President calls Parliament to meet. Prorogation: terminates a session. Dissolution: ends the life of Lok Sabha. Only Lok Sabha can be dissolved. Rajya Sabha is permanent. Minimum two sessions per year, gap not exceeding 6 months.

nodes.label: Party Whip
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Official appointed by party to ensure members attend sessions and vote according to party line. Three-line whip is most strict — defiance can lead to disqualification under anti-defection law. Important for maintaining party discipline.

nodes.label: Collegium System
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: System evolved through judicial interpretation (Second and Third Judges Cases, 1993 and 1998). CJI along with 4 senior-most SC judges recommend names for appointment. Established principle of collegiality. Not mentioned in Constitution but emerged from interpretation of consultation in Articles 124 and 217.

nodes.label: Gram Panchayat
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Base level of the three-tier Panchayati Raj system. Covers a village or group of villages. Members directly elected by the people. Five-year term. Around 2,50,000 Gram Panchayats exist in rural India. Headed by Sarpanch. Responsible for local governance, development, and welfare functions as devolved by the state.

nodes.label: Block/Mandal/Taluka Panchayat
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Intermediary level of the three-tier Panchayati Raj system. Also called Mandal or Taluka Panchayat. Need not be constituted in smaller states. About 6,000 block/intermediary Panchayats exist across India. Links Gram Panchayats with the Zilla Panchayat.

nodes.label: Zilla Panchayat
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Apex level of the three-tier Panchayati Raj system covering the entire rural area of a district. Nearly 500 Zilla Panchayats exist in India. Headed by Adhyaksha (Chairperson). At least 200 women serve as Adhyakshas of Zilla Panchayats. Coordinates development activities at district level.

nodes.label: Gram Sabha
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Comprises all adult members registered as voters in the Panchayat area. Mandatory creation under 73rd amendment. Its role and functions are decided by state legislation. In scheduled/tribal areas, the Gram Sabha has enhanced powers -- elected panchayats must get its consent in many respects. The democratic forum of the entire village.

nodes.label: Urban Local Bodies (Nagarpalikas)
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Three types based on size: Nagar Panchayat (transitional area), Municipal Council (smaller urban area), Municipal Corporation (larger urban area). Over 100 city corporations, 1400 town municipalities, and 2000+ Nagar Panchayats exist. Headed by elected Mayors/Chairpersons. Functions include urban planning, public health, water supply, roads, and sanitation.

nodes.label: Financial Constraints of Local Bodies
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Local bodies have very little funds of their own. Rural local bodies raise only 0.24% of total revenues but account for 4% of total government expenditure. Heavy dependence on state and central governments for financial support has eroded their capacity to operate effectively. Remain largely agencies implementing central and state welfare schemes rather than autonomous decision-making bodies.

nodes.label: Venkatachaliah Commission (2000)
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Commission to Review the Working of the Constitution, appointed in 2000 under retired CJI Justice Venkatachaliah. Opposition parties and many organisations boycotted it. Despite political controversy, the commission adhered to the basic structure theory and did not suggest measures endangering it. Shows the significance of basic structure doctrine in constitutional practice.

nodes.label: Creamy Layer Concept
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Introduced by the Supreme Court in the Indra Sawhney case (1992) regarding OBC reservations. Persons belonging to the more affluent or advanced sections within OBCs (creamy layer) are not entitled to benefits under reservations. Not applicable to SC/ST reservations. An example of how judicial interpretation evolves the Constitution without formal amendment.

nodes.label: 50% Ceiling on Reservations
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: In multiple decisions, the Supreme Court held that reservations in jobs and educational institutions cannot exceed 50% of total seats. This has become an accepted principle of Indian constitutional law. Not explicitly stated in the Constitution but established through judicial interpretation. An instance of informal constitutional evolution.

nodes.label: Political Theory
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Systematic study of political life including concepts like freedom, equality, justice, rights, and democracy. Provides a framework for evaluating political institutions and practices. UPSC tests the distinction between political theory and political science, and the normative vs empirical dimensions.

nodes.label: The State
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Community of persons permanently occupying a definite territory, independent of external control, possessing an organized government. Four elements: population, territory, government, sovereignty. UPSC 2021 tested this exact definition.

nodes.label: Government
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Agency through which the state exercises authority. Different from state: governments change, state endures. Forms include monarchy, aristocracy, democracy. UPSC tests the distinction between state and government.

nodes.label: Democracy
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Government by the people through elected representatives. Calls into activity the intelligence and character of ordinary men and women. Direct and representative forms. UPSC 2017 tested democracy's superior virtue.

nodes.label: Constitutional Government
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Government limited by terms of Constitution. Places restrictions on authority of state in interest of individual liberty, not on individual liberty in interest of state. UPSC 2021, 2020, 2014 tested this.

nodes.label: Political Philosophy
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Normative branch asking what ought to be: justice, good society, legitimate power. Distinguished from empirical political science. Thinkers include Plato, Aristotle, Hobbes, Locke, Rousseau, Marx.

nodes.label: Normative Approach
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Approach focusing on values, ideals, and what ought to be. Deals with justice, liberty, equality. Contrasted with empirical approach focusing on observable facts and behavior.

nodes.label: Plato
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Greek philosopher (428-348 BCE). Author of 'The Republic' exploring justice, ideal state, philosopher-kings. Justice means each part performing its proper function. Foundational to political philosophy.

nodes.label: Aristotle
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Greek philosopher (384-322 BCE), student of Plato. 'Father of Political Science'. Classified governments into monarchy, aristocracy, polity and corrupt forms. Man is a political animal.

nodes.label: Justice (Concept)
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Central concept. Plato: each part performing its proper function. Modern: distributive (fair allocation), procedural (fair processes), corrective (rectifying wrongs).

nodes.label: Power
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Ability to influence or control behavior. Weber's classification: traditional, charismatic, rational-legal authority. Must be accountable in democracy.

nodes.label: Liberty (Introduction)
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Opportunity to develop oneself fully, not merely absence of restraint. UPSC 2019: liberty is opportunity for self-development. Law and liberty complementary: no laws means no liberty (UPSC 2018).

nodes.label: Freedom
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Absence of external constraints combined with conditions enabling self-development. Not mere absence of restraint but presence of conditions for realizing one's potential. UPSC 2019: most appropriate definition is 'opportunity to develop oneself fully'.

nodes.label: Law and Liberty Relationship
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Law and liberty are complementary, not opposed. Without laws, there is no liberty because the strong would dominate the weak. Laws protect the freedom of all by restraining those who would violate others' freedom. UPSC 2018 tested: if there are no laws, there is no liberty.

nodes.label: Social Constraints on Freedom
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Freedom is constrained not only by state but also by social norms, customs, caste, gender, and religion. NCERT emphasizes that formal legal freedom is insufficient if social constraints like caste discrimination or patriarchy persist.

nodes.label: Liberty vs License
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Freedom is not the same as doing whatever one pleases (license). True liberty requires discipline, self-restraint, and respect for others' freedom. Liberty within the framework of law and social responsibility.

nodes.label: Freedom-Equality Tension
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Classical debate: expanding equality may require restricting freedom of some. Libertarians prioritize freedom over equality; socialists prioritize equality. NCERT argues they are complementary: substantive freedom requires basic equality of conditions.

nodes.label: Gandhi on Freedom
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Gandhi's concept of swaraj: self-rule at both national and individual level. Freedom as self-discipline and moral autonomy, not just political independence. Freedom connected to duty and responsibility. Linked to his vision of a stateless society.

nodes.label: Marx on Freedom
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Marx argued formal/legal freedoms are meaningless without economic equality. Bourgeois freedom protects property rights of the rich. True freedom requires abolition of class exploitation. Freedom is possible only in a classless society.

nodes.label: National Freedom / Self-Determination
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Freedom of a nation from external domination or colonial rule. Distinct from individual freedom. India's freedom movement was about national self-determination. After independence, the challenge shifted to securing individual freedoms within the free nation.

nodes.label: Equality
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Absence of special privileges and adequate opportunities for all. Does not mean sameness or identical treatment but equal consideration of interests. Implies absence of privileges (UPSC 2017). Foundational value of modern democracies.

nodes.label: Political Equality
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Equal political rights for all citizens: right to vote, contest elections, hold public office. Universal adult suffrage is the primary expression. One person, one vote, one value. Necessary but not sufficient for true equality.

nodes.label: Economic Equality
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Reduction of vast disparities in wealth, income, and property. Does not mean absolute equal distribution but minimum standard of living for all. Addressed in Indian Constitution through DPSPs, not Fundamental Rights. UPSC 2017: economic liberty is NOT in Preamble.

nodes.label: Legal Equality
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Equal treatment before law and equal protection of laws. No person is above the law. Article 14 of Indian Constitution embodies this. Combines British 'rule of law' concept with American 'equal protection of laws'.

nodes.label: Equality of Outcome
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Socialist ideal that results should also be equalized, not just starting conditions. Criticized by liberals as requiring excessive state intervention and suppressing individual liberty. Marxist and socialist perspective.

nodes.label: Formal Equality
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Equal treatment by law regardless of circumstances. Treating everyone identically. Criticized as insufficient because it ignores existing inequalities. Laws neutral on face but discriminatory in effect.

nodes.label: Substantive Equality
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Going beyond formal equal treatment to address real-world inequalities. May require differential treatment (affirmative action) to achieve genuine equality. Indian reservation policy is an example of pursuing substantive equality.

nodes.label: Feminism and Equality
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Feminist critique that formal equality ignores patriarchal structures. Gender equality requires addressing systemic discrimination, not just legal provisions. NCERT discusses how equal treatment of unequal situations perpetuates inequality.

nodes.label: Marxist View of Equality
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Marx argued that political and legal equality is meaningless without economic equality. Capitalism creates formal equality while maintaining class exploitation. True equality requires abolition of private property and class distinctions.

nodes.label: Procedural Justice
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Fairness of the processes and procedures used to make decisions. Due process of law is an example. UPSC 2023: 'Due Process of Law' means the principle of natural justice. Distinct from substantive or outcome-based justice.

nodes.label: Due Process of Law
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Principle of natural justice requiring fair legal procedures before depriving anyone of life, liberty, or property. UPSC 2023 tested this directly. American concept vs Indian 'procedure established by law'. Maneka Gandhi case (1978) brought India closer to due process.

nodes.label: Inclusive Governance
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Governance that includes all sections of society in decision-making and benefits. Involves effective district planning committees, government spending on public health, strengthening mid-day meal scheme. UPSC 2012 tested what constitutes inclusive governance.

nodes.label: Marx on Justice
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Marx's dialectical materialism explains class struggle as driver of history. Justice requires abolition of class exploitation and private property. From each according to ability, to each according to need. Communist Manifesto written with Engels. UPSC 2011 and 2006 tested this.

nodes.label: Gandhi on Justice
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Gandhi's concept of sarvodaya (welfare of all). Trusteeship theory: wealthy should act as trustees of their wealth for society. Non-violence as means to justice. Common ground with Marxism: final goal of stateless society (UPSC 2020).

nodes.label: Gandhism vs Marxism
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Common agreement: final goal of stateless society (UPSC 2020). Differences: Gandhi opposed class struggle and violence; Marx advocated revolution. Gandhi favored trusteeship; Marx favored abolition of private property. Gandhi was spiritual; Marx was materialist.

nodes.label: Reservation and Social Justice
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Constitutional provision for reservation of seats in education and public employment for SC, ST, and OBCs. Article 15(4), 16(4). Not a violation of equality but its fulfilment. Supreme Court in Indra Sawhney (1992) set 50% ceiling.

nodes.label: Rights
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Claims of citizens against the state, recognized and enforced by law. Rights are not privileges but entitlements essential for leading a life of dignity. UPSC 2017: rights are claims of citizens against the state (not state against citizens, not privileges).

nodes.label: Rights and Duties Relationship
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Rights and duties are correlated: one person's right implies another's duty. Citizen's right to free speech implies state's duty not to censor. But enjoyment of rights is NOT conditional on performance of duties. NCERT makes this distinction clearly.

nodes.label: Right to Vote
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Right to participate in elections. In India, it is a constitutional right (Article 326), not a fundamental right. UPSC 2017 tested this distinction: right to vote is a constitutional right, not fundamental or natural right.

nodes.label: Minority Rights
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Special rights for minority groups to protect their identity, culture, and language. Constitution recognizes religious and linguistic minorities (UPSC 1999). Articles 29-30 protect minority rights. Can establish and administer educational institutions.

nodes.label: Expansion of Rights
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Rights have expanded over time: from property rights to political rights to social/economic rights to environmental rights. Courts interpret existing rights broadly (e.g., Article 21 expanded to include privacy, shelter, livelihood). Dynamic process.

nodes.label: Citizenship
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Full and equal membership of a political community with associated rights and duties. More than legal status: implies active participation in public life. India has single citizenship. UPSC 2021 tested: India has only one citizenship and one domicile.

nodes.label: Citizenship by Descent
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Jus sanguinis principle: acquiring citizenship through parents. A person born outside India can be a citizen if parents are Indian citizens. Important for overseas Indian communities.

nodes.label: Citizenship by Naturalization
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Foreigners can acquire Indian citizenship after residing in India for a specified period and meeting other conditions. A naturalized citizen CAN be deprived of citizenship under certain circumstances (UPSC 2005, 2021 tested this).

nodes.label: Loss of Citizenship
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Three ways: voluntary renunciation, termination (acquiring citizenship of another country), deprivation (by government order if citizenship obtained by fraud, disloyalty, or trading with enemy). Naturalized citizens can be deprived; born citizens generally cannot.

nodes.label: Active Citizenship
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Going beyond passive legal status to active participation in democratic life. Includes voting, community engagement, holding government accountable. NCERT emphasizes this as essential for healthy democracy. Democratic decentralization enables active citizenship.

nodes.label: T.H. Marshall's Citizenship Theory
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: British sociologist who identified three dimensions of citizenship: civil (individual freedoms, 18th century), political (right to vote, 19th century), social (welfare, education, 20th century). Progressive expansion of citizenship rights.

nodes.label: Inclusive Citizenship
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Citizenship that includes all members regardless of caste, gender, religion, ethnicity. Historically, citizenship was restricted (women, slaves, lower castes excluded). Modern democracies strive for universal inclusive citizenship.

nodes.label: Civic Virtues
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Qualities citizens should possess: tolerance, respect for diversity, willingness to participate, concern for common good. NCERT emphasizes that democracy requires not just institutions but a democratic citizenry with these virtues.

nodes.label: Democratic Decentralization
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Devolution of power to local bodies (panchayats, municipalities). Local self-government is an exercise in democratic decentralization (UPSC 2017). Enables active citizenship by bringing government closer to people.

nodes.label: Duties of Citizens
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Obligations accompanying citizenship rights: obey laws, pay taxes, defend the country, respect Constitution. Fundamental Duties (Part IVA) list citizen obligations. However, enjoyment of rights is not conditional upon performing duties.

nodes.label: Protection of Minorities
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Secularism requires protecting minorities from majority domination. Articles 29-30 protect linguistic and religious minorities. National Commission for Minorities oversees. India recognizes religious AND linguistic minorities (UPSC 1999).

nodes.label: Satyagraha
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Gandhi's method of non-violent resistance: holding onto truth. Not passive resistance but active confrontation with injustice through peaceful means. Includes civil disobedience, non-cooperation, fasting. Boycott as political protest derived from a person's name (UPSC 1996).

nodes.label: Human Security
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Security of individuals, not just states. Includes economic security, food security, health security, environmental security, personal security. Broader than traditional military security. UNDP Human Development Report 1994 articulated this concept.

nodes.label: Development
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Process of economic growth, social progress, and improvement in quality of life. Not just GDP growth but overall human well-being. Political theory examines who benefits from development, at whose cost, and who decides. Central UPSC topic bridging polity and economics.

nodes.label: Economic Growth vs Development
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Growth measures increase in GDP/national income. Development is broader: includes health, education, equality, political freedoms. A country can have high growth but poor development (high inequality, low human development). NCERT makes this crucial distinction.

nodes.label: Amartya Sen
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Indian economist and philosopher. 'Development as Freedom' (1999). Development means expanding substantive freedoms: political, economic, social opportunities. Capability approach: what people are able to do and be, not just income. Nobel Prize 1998.

nodes.label: Capability Approach
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Amartya Sen's framework: evaluate development by what people are capable of doing and being (functionings and capabilities). Not just resources available but actual ability to lead the kind of life one values. Addresses both poverty and freedom.

nodes.label: Development vs Environment
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Tension between economic development and environmental protection. Industrialization degrades environment; environmental protection may slow growth. NCERT discusses: who bears environmental costs (usually the poor and tribal communities)?

nodes.label: Development-Induced Displacement
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Large development projects (dams, mines, highways) displace communities, particularly tribals and the poor. Narmada Bachao Andolan is prominent example. Raises questions: who benefits from development and who pays the cost?

nodes.label: Modernization Theory
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Theory that development follows a linear path from traditional to modern society, modeled on Western experience. Criticized for assuming Western path is universal, ignoring exploitation and colonialism. NCERT questions this assumption.

nodes.label: Dependency Theory
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Theory that underdevelopment of Global South results from exploitation by developed countries. Colonial extraction of resources, unfair trade, debt traps keep poor countries dependent. Contrasts with modernization theory. Latin American scholars like Andre Gunder Frank.

nodes.label: Planning and Development
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: State-directed economic planning as a model of development. India adopted Five Year Plans (1951-2017). Planning Commission replaced by NITI Aayog (2015). Debate between state-led and market-led development.

nodes.label: Globalization and Development
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Integration of world economies through trade, investment, technology. Proponents: raises living standards, spreads technology. Critics: widens inequality, destroys local industries, exploits developing countries. UPSC 1997 tested globalization and socialist ideology.

nodes.label: Welfare State
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: State that provides minimum standards of income, health, education, housing for all citizens as political right. DPSPs in Indian Constitution envision welfare state. Includes social security, public healthcare, free education.

nodes.label: Alternative Development Models
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Critiques of mainstream development: Gandhi's village-centered economy, environmentalism, feminist economics, indigenous knowledge systems. Development need not follow Western industrial model. NCERT discusses alternatives that prioritize community, environment, and equity.

nodes.label: Gandhi's Development Vision
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Gandhi envisioned decentralized village economy, self-sufficiency (swadeshi), cottage industries. Opposed large-scale industrialization as exploitative. Trusteeship model for wealth. Development should serve the last person (antyodaya). Alternative to Western industrialization.

nodes.label: Inequality and Development
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Development often increases inequality: benefits accrue to those already privileged while costs fall on marginalized. Income inequality, regional disparities, caste and gender gaps persist despite growth. Inclusive development aims to spread benefits equitably.

nodes.label: Boris Yeltsin
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: First elected President of Russia (1991-1999). Opposed the 1991 coup attempt, emerged as national hero. Led the dissolution of the Soviet Union. Blamed for hardships suffered during transition from communism to capitalism.

nodes.label: Unipolar World
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: After the USSR's collapse, the US became the sole superpower. Capitalist economy became dominant internationally. Institutions like World Bank and IMF became powerful advisors. Liberal democracy emerged as the preferred political system globally.

nodes.label: Multipolar World Order
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Vision shared by Russia and India of co-existence of several powers, collective security, greater regionalism, negotiated settlements, independent foreign policies, and strengthened UN. Alternative to US-dominated unipolar system.

nodes.label: Central Asian Republics
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan, and Uzbekistan gained independence after USSR's collapse. Rich in hydrocarbon resources. Became zone of competition between Russia, China, and the US. Several experienced authoritarian rule and civil conflicts.

nodes.label: Consequences of Cold War's End
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Three major consequences: end of ideological confrontation and arms race; shift to US-dominated unipolar system with capitalist economy dominant; emergence of many new independent countries from the former Soviet bloc with their own aspirations.

nodes.label: US Hegemony
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: US dominance in world politics after 1991 across three dimensions: hard power (military), structural power (economic institutions like World Bank, IMF, WTO), and soft power (cultural influence, ideology of liberal democracy). The US spends more on military than the next 12 powers combined.

nodes.label: Hegemony as Hard Power
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: US military dominance is both absolute and relative. Can reach any point on the planet accurately and in real time. Spends more on military than next 12 powers combined. Weakness lies in inability to police occupied territories effectively.

nodes.label: Hegemony as Soft Power
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: US cultural dominance and ability to manufacture consent. American ideas of good life, personal success, blue jeans, and burgers shape global aspirations. During the Cold War, US soft power undermined Soviet society. Called the most seductive culture on earth.

nodes.label: Bandwagon Strategy
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Strategy of extracting benefits by operating within the hegemonic system rather than opposing it. Working with the hegemon for trade, technology transfers, and investment. Alternative to directly challenging US power.

nodes.label: Guantanamo Bay
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: US Naval base in Cuba used to detain suspects in the War on Terror. Prisoners did not enjoy protection of international law or US law. Even UN representatives were denied access. Symbol of US unilateralism.

nodes.label: Euro
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Common European currency introduced in January 2002 in 12 EU member states. Can pose a threat to the dominance of the US dollar. Denmark and Sweden resisted adoption. Symbol of economic integration.

nodes.label: ASEAN Community
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: In 2003, ASEAN agreed to establish a community with three pillars: ASEAN Security Community, ASEAN Economic Community, and ASEAN Socio-Cultural Community. Vision 2020 defines outward-looking role. Unlike EU, no desire for supranational structures.

nodes.label: EU Limitations
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Member states have their own foreign and defence policies, often at odds (UK supported Iraq invasion while France and Germany opposed). Euro-scepticism in parts of Europe. Failed attempt at EU Constitution. Limits ability to act as unified entity.

nodes.label: Democracy in Nepal
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Hindu kingdom that became constitutional monarchy. King accepted new democratic constitution in 1990. Maoist insurgency and triangular conflict between monarchists, democrats, and Maoists. King abolished parliament in 2002. Massive pro-democracy protests in April 2006 forced restoration of democracy.

nodes.label: UN Security Council Reform
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Demands to expand permanent and non-permanent membership to reflect contemporary realities. Criteria proposed include: major economic/military power, substantial UN budget contributor, large population, democratic credentials, geographical diversity. No consensus on reform method.

nodes.label: UN 2005 Reform Proposals
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: At the 60th anniversary summit in 2005, leaders agreed on: Peacebuilding Commission, Responsibility to Protect doctrine, Human Rights Council (operational June 2006), Millennium Development Goals, condemnation of terrorism, Democracy Fund, winding up Trusteeship Council.

nodes.label: Terrorism as Security Threat
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Political violence targeting civilians deliberately and indiscriminately. International terrorism involves citizens or territory of more than one country. Classic cases include hijacking planes and bombs in public places. Gained prominence after 9/11 but is not new.

nodes.label: Global Poverty as Security Threat
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Half the world's population growth in six countries (India, China, Pakistan, Nigeria, Bangladesh, Indonesia). Disparity between North and South. Poverty drives migration, creating political frictions. Distinction between migrants (voluntary) and refugees (fleeing war/persecution).

nodes.label: Health Epidemics as Security Threat
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: HIV-AIDS, bird flu, SARS spread across countries through migration, business, tourism. By 2003, 4 crore infected with HIV-AIDS worldwide, two-thirds in Africa. New diseases like ebola emerged. Old diseases mutated into drug-resistant forms. Demonstrates growing interdependence.

nodes.label: Common but Differentiated Responsibilities
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Principle accepted at the 1992 Rio Declaration. Developed countries bear greater responsibility for environmental degradation due to historical emissions. Developing countries' special needs must be considered. India and China were exempted from Kyoto Protocol requirements.

nodes.label: North-South Divide on Environment
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Northern states concerned with ozone depletion and global warming. Southern states want to address relationship between economic development and environmental management. Developed countries want equal responsibility; developing countries argue historical polluters should bear more.

nodes.label: Oil and Resource Geopolitics
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Oil is the most important resource in global strategy. West Asia/Gulf region accounts for 30% of global production but 64% of known reserves. Saudi Arabia has a quarter of world reserves. Iraq has second largest. Resource competition has been a key driver of wars and alliances.

nodes.label: Globalisation
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Multi-dimensional concept dealing with flows of ideas, capital, commodities, and people creating worldwide interconnectedness. Has political, economic, and cultural manifestations. Not purely economic or cultural. Impact is vastly uneven across societies. Has historical roots but contemporary speed and scale are unique.

nodes.label: Economic Globalisation
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Greater economic flows among countries including trade in commodities, capital movement, and FDI. Reduction of import restrictions and capital controls. IMF and WTO play key roles. Developed countries guard borders with visa policies while promoting free movement of capital. Creates intense division of opinion.

nodes.label: Political Consequences of Globalisation
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Erosion of state capacity as welfare state gives way to minimalist state. Market becomes prime determinant. MNCs reduce government decision-making ability. However, state capacity also enhanced by technology for surveillance. States continue to discharge essential functions.

nodes.label: Cultural Consequences of Globalisation
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Fear of cultural homogenisation through imposition of Western (especially American) culture. McDonaldisation of the world. But also generates cultural heterogenisation, making each culture more distinctive. Cultural exchange is rarely one-way. Burger does not replace masala dosa; jeans combine with khadi kurta.

nodes.label: Cultural Homogenisation
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Fear that globalisation leads to uniform culture dominated by Western/American values. McDonaldisation. Blue jeans and burgers as symbols. Dangerous for cultural heritage diversity. But countered by cultural heterogenisation where cultures become more distinctive.

nodes.label: Technology and Globalisation
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Telegraph, telephone, and microchip revolutionised communication. Technology enables faster movement of ideas, capital, commodities, and people. Internet and computer services exemplify idea flows. Printing created nationalism; technology now shapes collective lives.

nodes.label: Resistance to Globalisation
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Left critics: globalisation makes rich richer and poor poorer, weakens state capacity to protect the poor. Right critics: fear weakening of state, want protectionism, worry about cultural erosion. Anti-globalisation movements participate in global networks themselves. Many oppose specific programmes, not globalisation per se.

nodes.label: India's Resistance to Globalisation
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Left wing protests through political parties and Indian Social Forum. Trade unions and farmer organisations opposed MNC entry. Opposition to patenting of plants like Neem by foreign firms. Right wing objections to cultural influences: foreign TV channels, Valentine's Day, westernisation of dress.

nodes.label: Decline of Welfare State
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Globalisation leads to the old welfare state giving way to minimalist state performing only core functions (law and order, security). Market becomes prime determinant of economic and social priorities. Social safety nets advocated to protect the economically weak.

nodes.label: Role of Multinational Corporations (MNCs)
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: MNCs reduce government capacity for independent decisions. Drive economic globalisation through trade and investment. Their entry into developing countries raises concerns about local industry survival. Example: retail chains threatening small shopkeepers.

nodes.label: Social Safety Nets
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Institutional safeguards to minimise negative effects of globalisation on economically weak populations. Those concerned about social justice emphasise their need. Many movements argue safety nets are insufficient or unworkable.

nodes.label: Demand for Separate States
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Various movements demanding creation of new states -- Gorkhaland from West Bengal, Chhattisgarh from MP, Jharkhand from Bihar, Uttaranchal from UP. Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand and Uttarakhand were created in 2000. These represent the ongoing challenge of accommodating regional aspirations.

nodes.label: National Democratic Alliance (NDA)
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: BJP-led coalition that governed India from 1998-2004 under PM Atal Behari Vajpayee. Included diverse regional parties that did not necessarily agree with Hindutva ideology. The 1999 NDA government completed its full term. Demonstrated that coalition politics could provide stable governance.

nodes.label: United Progressive Alliance (UPA)
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Congress-led coalition that won the 2004 elections, defeating NDA. Received support from Left Front parties. Represented the partial revival of Congress. In the 2004 election, there was negligible difference between the votes of Congress allies and BJP allies.

nodes.label: Four-Point Political Consensus
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Broad agreement emerging among most parties after 1990s: (1) acceptance of new economic policies, (2) acceptance of OBC social and political claims, (3) acceptance of state-level parties' role in national governance, and (4) emphasis on pragmatic considerations over ideology in coalition-making.

nodes.label: Kerala - Cultural Diversity
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: A coastal state in south-west India. Spice trade attracted Jewish, Arab, and Portuguese traders. Christianity arrived via St. Thomas nearly 2000 years ago. People practise Judaism, Islam, Christianity, Hinduism, and Buddhism. Chinese fishing nets (cheena-vala) reflect Chinese influence.

nodes.label: Levels of Government
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Government works at three levels: local (village, town, locality), state (entire state like Haryana or Assam), and national (entire country). Each level handles matters appropriate to its jurisdiction and scope.

nodes.label: Monarchy
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: A form of government where the monarch (king or queen) holds decision-making power. The monarch may consult with a small group but retains final authority. Unlike democracy, monarchs do not have to explain their actions or defend their decisions.

nodes.label: Government Services
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: The government runs essential services including postal services, railways, disaster relief, health facilities, and social programmes for the poor. Institutions like the Supreme Court, Indian Railways, and Bharat Petroleum are part of the government.

nodes.label: Equality and Justice
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: A key idea of democratic government -- equality and justice are inseparable. The government recognises unequal groups in society and makes special provisions for them. For example, fee waivers for girls in government schools to overcome gender injustice.
nodes.chapter_title: Key Elements of a Democratic Government

nodes.label: Apartheid in South Africa
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: A system of racial separation in South Africa where people were divided into white, black, Indian, and coloured races. Non-whites could not vote, were denied equal facilities (hospitals, ambulances, transport), and were restricted to the worst land. Abolished in 1994 with democracy.
nodes.chapter_title: Key Elements of a Democratic Government

nodes.label: Nelson Mandela
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: The most well-known leader of the African National Congress who fought against apartheid in South Africa for several years. His struggle succeeded in 1994 when South Africa became a democratic country where people of all races were considered equal.
nodes.chapter_title: Key Elements of a Democratic Government

nodes.label: Special Provisions for Equality
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: The government makes special provisions for unequal groups in society to promote justice. For instance, waiving or lowering fees for girls in government schools and colleges to counter the societal tendency to value boy children more than girl children.
nodes.chapter_title: Key Elements of a Democratic Government

nodes.label: Sarpanch (Panchayat President)
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: The elected head of the Gram Panchayat, also known as the Panchayat President. Elected by all members of the Gram Sabha. The Sarpanch leads Gram Panchayat meetings and presides over decision-making on village development matters.

nodes.label: Ward Members (Panchs)
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Elected representatives of wards (smaller areas) within a village Panchayat. Each ward elects one Ward Member or Panch. Together with the Sarpanch, they form the Gram Panchayat and are answerable to the Gram Sabha.

nodes.label: Panchayat Secretary
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: An appointed (not elected) government official who serves as Secretary of both the Gram Sabha and Gram Panchayat. Responsible for calling meetings of the Gram Sabha and Gram Panchayat and keeping a record of proceedings.

nodes.label: Panchayat Samiti (Block Level)
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: The second tier of Panchayati Raj at the block level, also called Janpad Panchayat. It has many Gram Panchayats under it and coordinates development at the block level. It helps regulate money distribution among Gram Panchayats.

nodes.label: Zila Parishad (District Level)
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: The third and highest tier of Panchayati Raj at the district level, also called District Panchayat. It makes developmental plans at the district level and regulates money distribution among all Gram Panchayats with the help of Panchayat Samitis.

nodes.label: Three-Tier Panchayat Structure
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: The Panchayati Raj system operates at three levels: Gram Panchayat (village), Panchayat Samiti/Janpad Panchayat (block), and Zila Parishad/District Panchayat (district). This extends the idea of people participation from village to district level.

nodes.label: Below Poverty Line (BPL) List
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: A list of families living below the poverty line that must be approved by the Gram Sabha. The list determines who receives government benefits for the poor. The Gram Sabha can challenge incorrect entries and ensure genuinely poor families are included.

nodes.label: Gram Sabha Oversight Role
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: The Gram Sabha is a key factor in making the Gram Panchayat accountable. It prevents the Panchayat from misusing money or favouring certain people. All plans for Panchayat work are placed before the Gram Sabha for approval.

nodes.label: Sources of Panchayat Funds
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Panchayats get funds from three sources: collection of taxes on houses and market places, government scheme funds received through various departments via Janpad and Zila Panchayats, and donations for community works.

nodes.label: Watershed Development
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: A programme for water conservation and recharging groundwater, involving planting trees, constructing check-dams and tanks. The government provides funds for this work. It can transform barren slopes into green meadows in just two years.

nodes.label: Block Development Officer
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: A government officer at the block level who provides information and support for development schemes. The Gram Panchayat approaches the BDO for details on government programmes like watershed development.

nodes.label: Land Records
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Records maintained by the Patwari showing who owns what land, plot measurements, crops grown, and facilities. The Khasra record identifies plot ownership. These records are essential for land disputes, sales, loans, and property division. Some states are computerising these records.

nodes.label: Tehsildar (Revenue Officer)
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: A revenue officer who works under the District Collector. Tehsildars hear land disputes, supervise the work of Patwaris, ensure records are properly kept and land revenue is collected. They also handle caste certificates and other administrative matters.

nodes.label: District Collector
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: The head of district administration for land and revenue matters. Revenue officers (Tehsildars) work under the District Collector. The Collector oversees land records, revenue collection, and dispute resolution at the district level.

nodes.label: Women Land Rights
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Historically, women were seen as workers on land but not owners of agricultural land. Till recently, Hindu women in some states did not get a share in family agricultural land. The Hindu Succession Amendment Act 2005 changed this by granting equal inheritance rights.

nodes.label: Municipal Corporation
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: The urban local body responsible for large cities. Handles street lights, garbage collection, water supply, street cleaning, disease prevention, running schools and hospitals, and maintaining gardens. Smaller towns have a Municipal Council instead.

nodes.label: Municipal Council
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: The urban local body for smaller towns, performing similar functions as a Municipal Corporation but on a smaller scale. Both are forms of urban local self-government responsible for civic amenities and services.

nodes.label: Ward Councillor
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: An elected representative of a city ward in the Municipal Corporation. Ward Councillors make decisions about parks, hospitals, bus stands, and garbage collection through committees. They represent ward-level concerns before the entire council.

nodes.label: Municipal Commissioner
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: An appointed (not elected) officer who heads the administrative staff of the Municipal Corporation. While Councillors and their committees decide on issues, the Commissioner and administrative staff implement those decisions.

nodes.label: Property Tax
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: A tax paid by homeowners to the Municipal Corporation for services provided. The larger the house, the more the tax. Property taxes form only 25-30 per cent of Municipal Corporation revenue. Other taxes include education tax, entertainment tax, and commercial taxes.

nodes.label: Urban Wards
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Cities are divided into different wards for administrative purposes. Each ward elects a Ward Councillor. Wards allow local-level governance within the larger city, similar to how villages have ward members in panchayats.

nodes.label: Councillor Committees
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Groups of Ward Councillors who form committees to decide and debate city-wide issues like water supply, garbage collection, street lighting, and bus stand improvement. Complex decisions affecting the entire city are made through these committees.

nodes.label: Municipal Departments
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: The work in a city is divided into departments: water department, garbage collection, gardens, roads, sanitation, etc. Each department handles its specific area of urban services under the overall supervision of the Commissioner.

nodes.label: Community Protest and Accountability
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Citizens can hold the Municipal Corporation accountable through protests, petitions, and approaching their Ward Councillor. When garbage collection was neglected in certain localities, women organised protests and petition campaigns forcing the Corporation to act.

nodes.label: Sub-Contracting of Municipal Services
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: To save money, many municipalities hire private contractors to collect and process garbage. Contract workers get paid less, have temporary jobs, lack safety measures, and are not taken care of if injured while working. A growing trend in urban governance.

nodes.label: Urban Slums and Services
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Poor people in cities work as domestic servants and sanitation workers but live in slums without water and sanitation facilities. Municipal Corporations cite lack of land ownership and non-payment of taxes, yet middle-class areas pay little tax relative to services received.

nodes.label: Casual Workers
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Workers employed on an as-needed basis without job security or benefits. They work when the employer needs them (during large orders or certain seasons) and must find other work at other times. If they complain about pay or conditions, they are asked to leave.

nodes.label: Daily Wage Labourers (Labour Chowk)
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Workers who gather at labour chowk (crossings) waiting to be hired as helpers to masons, for construction, loading trucks, digging pipelines, or building roads. Thousands of such casual workers exist in cities. Many cannot afford permanent accommodation and sleep on pavements.

nodes.label: Factory Workers
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Workers in small workshops and factories, often employed on casual basis. In garment export units, workers work 9am to 10pm during peak months (Dec-Apr), six days a week. Cloth mill workers do 12-hour day and night shifts. Workers are laid off when orders decline.

nodes.label: Worker Benefits
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Benefits received by permanent workers include: provident fund (savings for old age with government interest), holidays (Sundays, national holidays, annual leave), medical facilities for family, and medical leave without salary cuts. Casual workers receive none of these.

nodes.label: Job Security
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: The key difference between permanent and casual employment. Permanent workers have job stability, cannot be easily dismissed, and receive benefits. Casual workers have no security, no protection against ill-treatment, and can be asked to leave anytime. Street vendors can be evicted by police.

nodes.label: Right to Health
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: According to the Constitution, it is the primary duty of the government to ensure welfare of people and provide healthcare facilities to all. The Supreme Court held that the Right to Life under Article 21 includes the right to health. Denial of timely medical treatment violates this protection.
nodes.chapter_title: Role of the Government in Health

nodes.label: Public Health Services
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: A chain of health centres and hospitals run by the government, funded by tax revenue. Covers rural and urban areas from village health centres to district hospitals. Meant to provide quality healthcare either free or at low cost so even the poor can access treatment.
nodes.chapter_title: Role of the Government in Health

nodes.label: Private Health Facilities
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Not owned or controlled by government. Includes private clinics, hospitals, nursing homes, laboratories, and medical shops. Patients must pay for every service. Increasingly dominant in India but concentrated in urban areas, leading to unequal access.
nodes.chapter_title: Role of the Government in Health

nodes.label: Healthcare Inequality in India
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Despite having the largest number of medical colleges globally and being the fourth largest medicine producer, healthcare remains unequal. Most doctors settle in urban areas. Only 20 percent of the population can afford all required medicines. 40 percent of hospitalised patients must borrow money or sell possessions.
nodes.chapter_title: Role of the Government in Health

nodes.label: Taxes and Public Services
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Government uses tax revenue to fund public services like defence, police, judiciary, highways, education, healthcare, and employment. Tax money is also used for disaster relief and developmental programmes. Services like healthcare are provided especially for the poor who cannot purchase them from the market.
nodes.chapter_title: Role of the Government in Health

nodes.label: Costa Rica Health Approach
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Costa Rica decided not to have an army and redirected military spending to health, education, and basic needs. The government provides safe drinking water, sanitation, nutrition, and housing to all citizens. Health education is integral at all levels of education.
nodes.chapter_title: Role of the Government in Health

nodes.label: Medical Ethics and Generic Medicines
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: The Medical Council of India Code of Medical Ethics requires physicians to prescribe drugs with generic names and ensure rational prescription. Some private practitioners prescribe unnecessary medicines and injections to earn more, increasing costs for patients.
nodes.chapter_title: Role of the Government in Health

nodes.label: DPSP - Health and Nutrition
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: The Constitution states it is the duty of the State to raise the level of nutrition and standard of living and to improve public health. This Directive Principle of State Policy provides the constitutional basis for government healthcare obligations though it is not judicially enforceable.
nodes.chapter_title: Role of the Government in Health

nodes.label: Womens Health Neglect
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Womens health concerns are often considered less important than mens in the family. Women are frequently not taken to doctors promptly. Many tribal areas lack proper health centres. Gender-based health discrimination compounds the problem of unequal healthcare access.
nodes.chapter_title: Role of the Government in Health

nodes.label: State Legislative Assembly (Vidhan Sabha)
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Every state in India has a Legislative Assembly where elected MLAs meet to discuss issues, ask questions, debate policies, decide on spending, and approve government decisions. It is the place where laws for the state are made and the executive is held accountable.

nodes.label: Member of Legislative Assembly (MLA)
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: MLAs are elected by people from constituencies into which each state is divided. They represent their constituents in the Legislative Assembly. Some MLAs have dual responsibilities as both legislators and ministers. MLAs belong to different political parties.

nodes.label: Ruling Party
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: The political party whose MLAs have won more than half the constituencies in a state gains a majority and becomes the ruling party. It forms the government. At times, the ruling party may be a coalition of parties working together to achieve a majority.

nodes.label: Opposition
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Elected representatives who are not members of the ruling party. They play the crucial role of questioning government decisions and actions, raising new issues for consideration in the Assembly, and holding the government accountable.

nodes.label: Executive (State Government)
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: The Chief Minister and other ministers who take decisions and run the government through various departments like Public Works, Agriculture, Health, and Education. In common usage government refers to this executive branch. They must get their decisions approved by the legislature.

nodes.label: Legislature (State Level)
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: All the MLAs who gather in the Legislative Assembly form the legislature. They authorise and supervise the work of the executive. The head of the executive (Chief Minister) is chosen from among them. They have the main authority in a democracy.

nodes.label: Debate in Legislative Assembly
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: MLAs can express opinions, ask questions, and give suggestions on current problems during Assembly debates. Ministers must reply to questions and assure the Assembly that adequate steps are being taken. This is a key mechanism of democratic accountability.

nodes.label: Press Conference
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: A gathering of journalists invited to hear about and ask questions on a particular issue, expected to report to the larger public. Ministers use press conferences to explain government actions. This is one way democratic accountability extends beyond the Assembly.

nodes.label: Government Departments
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: The executive works through departments like Public Works, Agriculture, Health, and Education. Ministers head these departments. Whatever work is done by departments must be approved by members of the Legislative Assembly.

nodes.label: State Lawmaking Power
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: The state government can make new laws for the state in the Legislative Assembly. For example, making it compulsory for municipal corporations to ensure adequate toilets, or appointing health workers in every village. Laws for the entire country are made in Parliament.

nodes.label: Democratic Accountability
nodes.subject: polity
