nodes.detail: In a democracy, people elect MLAs who form the government, and ministers must answer to the legislature. Through Assembly debates, press conferences, public protests, and media, the government is held accountable. People have the main authority as they elect representatives.

nodes.label: Gender Roles and Stereotypes
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Societies assign different roles to men and women, with mens work typically valued more. Boys are given cars and girls dolls; girls must talk softly while boys must be tough. These stereotypes limit career choices and life opportunities for both genders.
nodes.chapter_title: Growing Up as Boys and Girls

nodes.label: Housework as Invisible Unpaid Work
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Housework and caregiving are primarily done by women but not recognised as real work. It is physically demanding, time-consuming, and unpaid. Women spend much more time working than men when housework and paid work are combined, creating a double burden.
nodes.chapter_title: Growing Up as Boys and Girls

nodes.label: Double Burden of Women
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Women who work outside the home also bear the main responsibility for housework and caregiving. Data from the Central Statistical Organization (1998-99) shows women in Haryana work 53 hours per week (23 paid, 30 unpaid) compared to mens 40 hours (38 paid, 2 unpaid).
nodes.chapter_title: Growing Up as Boys and Girls

nodes.label: Lives of Domestic Workers
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Domestic workers, mostly women and sometimes children, perform sweeping, cleaning, washing, cooking, and caregiving. They face low wages, long hours (5 AM to midnight), lack of respect from employers, and poor working conditions. Domestic work is devalued by society.
nodes.chapter_title: Growing Up as Boys and Girls

nodes.label: Anganwadi (Child-Care Centres)
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Government-run child-care centres set up in several villages across the country. They reduce the burden of childcare on women, enabling them to take up employment outside the home and allowing more girls to attend school. Part of the ICDS scheme.
nodes.chapter_title: Growing Up as Boys and Girls

nodes.label: Creche Facilities - Legal Mandate
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: The government has passed laws making it mandatory for organisations with more than 30 women employees to provide creche facilities. This enables women to participate in the workforce and supports girls education by freeing them from childcare duties.
nodes.chapter_title: Growing Up as Boys and Girls

nodes.label: Gender and Access to Education
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: The burden of childcare and housework falling on women and girls directly impacts whether girls can attend school and whether women can work outside the home. Government interventions like anganwadis and creches aim to address this structural barrier.
nodes.chapter_title: Growing Up as Boys and Girls

nodes.label: Unequal Valuation of Mens and Womens Work
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: In most societies, roles men play and work they do are valued more highly than womens work. Housework requires heavy physical labour including bending, lifting, carrying, and standing for long hours, yet is not considered real work. This devaluation is a basis for gender inequality.
nodes.chapter_title: Growing Up as Boys and Girls

nodes.label: Womens Movement in India
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: A vibrant movement of individual women and womens organisations struggling for equality across spheres of legal reform, violence, health, and education. Uses strategies like campaigning, raising awareness through street plays and songs, protesting through rallies, and showing solidarity.

nodes.label: Gender Stereotypes in Work
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Many people believe women are suited only for certain jobs like nursing because they are patient and gentle, while science requires a technical mind women supposedly lack. 83.6 percent of working women in India are in agriculture yet farmers are imagined as male. These stereotypes limit career choices.

nodes.label: Discrimination
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: When people or organisations act on their prejudices and do not treat people equally or with respect. Takes place when someone is treated differently or distinctions are made based on gender, caste, religion, or other social identities.

nodes.label: Laxmi Lakra - Breaking Stereotypes
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: From a poor tribal family in Jharkhand, she became the first woman engine driver for Northern Railways at age 27. Her parents were not literate but ensured their children got education. She studied in a government school and got a diploma in electronics, challenging gender stereotypes at every step.

nodes.label: Parliamentary Approval and Accountability
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Parliament exercises control over the executive through question hour, debates, and no-confidence motions. The government must justify its actions to Parliament and maintain majority support. Can be removed if it loses confidence of the house.
nodes.chapter_title: Why Do We Need a Parliament

nodes.label: Law-Making Function of Parliament
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Parliament's central function is making laws. A bill must be passed by both houses and receive Presidential assent to become law. Parliament annually passes new laws and revises existing ones. It is sensitive to problems faced by people and translates concerns into legislation.
nodes.chapter_title: Why Do We Need a Parliament

nodes.label: Role of the Opposition
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Opposition parties question the government, highlight failures, and mobilise public opinion. They ensure healthy debate and prevent the ruling party from becoming autocratic. A strong opposition is essential for functioning democracy.
nodes.chapter_title: Why Do We Need a Parliament

nodes.label: Parliament and National Issues
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Parliament serves as the highest forum for discussion and debate on public issues and national policy. Members raise issues affecting their constituencies and the nation. Addresses concerns from economic policy to social justice.
nodes.chapter_title: Why Do We Need a Parliament

nodes.label: How New Laws Come About
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Process involves: groups raising need for law, nationwide consultations, drafting a bill, submission to Parliamentary Standing Committee, recommendations, introduction in Parliament, passage by both houses, and Presidential assent. Citizens play crucial role at every stage.

nodes.label: Parliamentary Standing Committee
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Committees examining bills referred to them. Receive submissions from civil society and affected groups, examine evidence, submit recommendations. Crucial for ensuring laws reflect diverse viewpoints before final passage.

nodes.label: Role of Citizens in Law-Making
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Citizens help Parliament frame concerns into laws. From establishing need to passage, citizen voice is crucial. TV reports, editorials, radio, local meetings make Parliament's work accessible. Citizens can lobby, petition, and protest.

nodes.label: Adivasis (Scheduled Tribes)
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Literally 'original inhabitants', communities living in close association with forests. About 8% of India's population. Over 500 different groups. Concentrated in Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand, MP, Odisha, Gujarat, Maharashtra, Rajasthan, AP, WB, and northeast states. Distinguished by lack of hierarchy, unlike caste-based communities.

nodes.label: Adivasi Displacement
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Over 50% of persons displaced by mining projects are tribals. 79% displaced in AP, Chhattisgarh, Odisha, Jharkhand are tribals. Huge tracts lost to dams and projects. Forced from forests declared as reserves or sanctuaries. When staying, termed encroachers. Displacement destroys traditional livelihoods and culture.

nodes.label: Adivasis and Forests
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Adivasis had deep knowledge of, access to, and control over vast forest tracts until mid-19th century. Forests provided metal ores, timber, medicinal herbs, animal products. Adivasis use ~10,000 plant species. Forest policies, economic changes, and political force have increasingly pushed them out over 200 years.

nodes.label: Stereotyping of Adivasis
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Adivasis invariably portrayed in colourful costumes, headgear, and dancing. Wrongly seen as exotic, primitive, and backward. Blamed for their lack of advancement as supposedly resistant to change. This stereotyping leads to discrimination and ignores the richness and diversity of their lives.

nodes.label: Muslims and Marginalisation
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: At 14.2% of population (2011 census), Muslims are considered marginalised due to deprivation of socio-economic development benefits. Lower access to basic amenities, lower literacy rates, and severe under-representation in public employment (3% IAS, 4% IPS, 1.8% IFS). Sachar Committee Report documented this comprehensively.

nodes.label: Social Marginalisation
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Discrimination based on distinct customs, practices, and identity. Muslim customs sometimes seen as different from 'mainstream', leading to stereotyping. Can lead to unfair treatment, ghettoisation, prejudice, and sometimes hatred and violence. Social and economic marginalisation are deeply interlinked.

nodes.label: Ghettoisation
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Process by which a community is concentrated in specific areas or localities due to social, cultural, economic reasons, or fear and hostility. Ghettoised communities have few options of moving out, leading to alienation from rest of society. Affects Muslims in some Indian cities.

nodes.label: Economic Marginalisation
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Deprivation from socio-economic development benefits. For Adivasis: 45% rural and 35% urban live below poverty line, children malnourished, low literacy. For Muslims: lower access to basic amenities and public employment. Economic and social marginalisation are interconnected dimensions.

nodes.label: Adivasi Migration
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: From 1830s, Adivasis migrated in large numbers to plantations worldwide - Mauritius, Caribbean, Australia. India's tea industry built on their labour in Assam (70 lakh Adivasis in Assam today). Five lakh perished in 19th century migrations alone. Modern displacement forces migration to cities for low-wage work.

nodes.label: Promoting Social Justice
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: State and central governments create specific schemes for tribal areas and Dalit populations. Examples include free/subsidised hostels for Dalit and Adivasi students, special scholarships, and targeted development programmes. Government operates through both laws and policies to end inequity.

nodes.label: Manual Scavenging
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Practice of removing human/animal waste from dry latrines and carrying it on the head. Mainly done by Dalit women and girls. About 1 lakh persons employed in 26 lakh dry latrines. Exposed to health hazards and very low wages. The 1993 Act prohibited it; the 2013 Act strengthened prohibition and provided for rehabilitation.

nodes.label: Dalits
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: The term means 'broken', deliberately used to highlight centuries of caste discrimination. Also referred to as Scheduled Castes in official documents. Face untouchability, social exclusion, economic deprivation. Constitution provides safeguards through Articles 15, 17, and reservation policies.

nodes.label: Adivasi Land Rights in Constitution
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: The Constitution guarantees that land belonging to tribal people cannot be sold to or bought by non-tribal people. Where this has happened, tribals have the right to re-possess their land. The SC/ST Act confirms these rights and allows activists to seek punishment for violators.

nodes.label: Right to Water
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: The Constitution recognises the right to water as part of the Right to Life under Article 21. Every person, rich or poor, should have sufficient water at an affordable price. Several High Court and Supreme Court cases have held safe drinking water is a Fundamental Right. The Andhra Pradesh HC reaffirmed this in 2007.

nodes.label: Government's Role in Public Facilities
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Government must bear responsibility for providing public facilities because private companies operate for profit and many public services offer no profit. Even where private companies provide facilities (schools, hospitals, water), they charge prices only some can afford. The Right to Life requires universal access.

nodes.label: Taxes and Government Revenue
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Government finances public facilities through taxes collected from people. The annual budget presented in Parliament accounts for government expenses and revenue. Main sources include corporation tax, income tax, customs, excise duties, and service tax. Some facilities also charge user fees set at affordable rates.

nodes.label: Water Supply Inequality
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Massive disparities in water access. Urban standard is 135 litres per person per day but slum dwellers get less than 20 litres (one bucket) while luxury hotels use up to 1,600 litres (80 buckets). The burden of water shortages falls disproportionately on the poor who cannot afford private alternatives.

nodes.label: Privatisation of Water Supply
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Some argue private companies should handle water supply since government is unable to meet demand. But globally, water supply is almost always a government function. Where privatised (Bolivia), steep price rises triggered riots. Mumbai and Hyderabad show success with government-run departments. Private involvement should be 'on contract' under government regulation.

nodes.label: Universal Access
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Achieved when everyone has physical access to a good and can also afford it. For example, a tap connection at home for physical access, and low or free pricing for affordability. Porto Alegre, Brazil achieved universal access to safe water leading to low infant deaths.

nodes.label: Sanitation as Public Facility
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Provision of facilities for safe disposal of waste. Sanitation coverage in India is even lower than water (only 36% households had toilets in 2001). The poor in rural and urban areas lack access most. Sulabh, an NGO, has constructed 7,500+ public toilet blocks and 1.2 million private toilets serving 10 million people.

nodes.label: Public Transport
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Buses are the most important form of public transport over short distances, linking working people to workplaces. With rapid urbanisation, bus systems have not kept pace. Government planned metro rail projects like Delhi Metro (Rs 11,000 crore for first segment). Mumbai suburban railway handles 65 lakh passengers daily over 300 km.

nodes.label: Water-Related Diseases
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: India has one of the largest number of diarrhoea, dysentery, and cholera cases. Over 1,600 Indians, mostly children under five, die daily from water-related diseases. These deaths are preventable with access to safe drinking water, making it a critical public health issue linked to Right to Life.

nodes.label: Porto Alegre Water Model
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: A city in Brazil that achieved universal access to safe water through a transparent public water department. Average price kept low, poor charged half the basic rate. Profits reinvested in improvements. People participate directly in deciding department priorities through public meetings. A model of successful public provision.

nodes.label: Environment as Public Facility
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: A clean environment is a public facility shared across generations that cannot be destroyed for industrial development. Court orders on environmental issues sometimes affect livelihoods (factory closures displacing workers). Challenge is finding solutions where workers' livelihoods are protected alongside clean environment.

nodes.label: IMF and World Bank
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: International financial institutions where voting power is based on financial contribution, not one-country-one-vote. US effectively holds veto power. Raises questions about democracy in global governance.

nodes.label: Michelle Bachelet
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Daughter of General Bachelet killed under Pinochet. Imprisoned and tortured. First woman Defence Minister in Latin America, elected President of Chile in 2006. Symbolises democracy's triumph.

nodes.label: Four Features of Democracy
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Democracy requires: (1) rulers elected by people take major decisions, (2) free and fair elections with real choice, (3) one person one vote one value, (4) government limited by constitutional law and citizens' rights. These four features distinguish true democracy from pretend-democracies.

nodes.label: Major Decisions by Elected Leaders
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: In a democracy, final decision-making power must rest with those elected by the people. Pakistan under Musharraf is an example where elected representatives existed but real power lay with the military, making it not a true democracy.

nodes.label: Free and Fair Elections
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Elections must offer real choice between political alternatives. Those in power must have a fair chance of losing. China's single-party elections and Mexico's PRI dominance (until 2000) are examples of unfair elections that do not qualify as democratic.

nodes.label: One Person One Vote One Value
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Each adult citizen must have one vote and each vote must have equal value. Violations include Saudi Arabia denying women voting rights (until 2015), Estonia's citizenship rules excluding Russian minorities, and Fiji's unequal weighting of votes.

nodes.label: Rule of Law in Democracy
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: A democratic government rules within limits set by constitutional law and citizens' rights. Zimbabwe under Mugabe illustrates how popular governments can be undemocratic if they violate rule of law, change constitutions to increase power, and suppress opposition.

nodes.label: Arguments for Democracy
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Democracy promotes equality, enhances individual dignity, improves decision-making quality through consultation, provides methods to resolve conflicts peacefully, and allows room to correct mistakes through elections.

nodes.label: Arguments against Democracy
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Critics argue: leaders keep changing leading to instability, elections lead to morality-free competition, ordinary people lack expertise for decision-making, delays in decision-making, and corruption. These criticisms are addressed by democracy's ability to self-correct.

nodes.label: Broader Definition of Democracy
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Beyond government, democracy is a principle applicable to families, schools, and all organisations. It involves decision-making by consent, respect for individual opinions, and elimination of discrimination based on caste, religion, gender, or economic status.

nodes.label: Accountability in Democracy
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Democratic governments are accountable to the people through elections, constitutional limits, and independent institutions. Every office bearer has rights and responsibilities assigned by constitution and law, accountable to both people and other independent officials.

nodes.label: Limits on Majority Rule
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: In a democracy, the majority cannot do whatever it likes. It must respect constitutional rules, guarantees to minorities, and follow consultative processes. Zimbabwe's Mugabe showed how majoritarian rule without limits becomes undemocratic.

nodes.label: Dictatorship
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: A form of government where rulers are not elected by people and exercise unlimited power. Examples include Pinochet's Chile, Myanmar's military junta, and Saudi Arabia's monarchy. Contrasted with democracy across all four features.

nodes.label: Need for a Constitution
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Constitution serves four functions: (1) generates trust and coordination among diverse people, (2) specifies how government will be constituted and powers distributed, (3) limits government power and defines citizen rights, (4) expresses aspirations about creating a good society.

nodes.label: Conditions for Democratic Election
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Five conditions: (1) universal franchise - one person one vote, (2) real choice among parties/candidates, (3) regular intervals, (4) preferred candidate gets elected, (5) free and fair conduct. Elections without these are not truly democratic.

nodes.label: Electoral Constituency
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Country divided into areas for elections; voters in each area elect one representative. India has 543 Lok Sabha constituencies. Each state divided into Assembly constituencies. Each constituency has roughly equal population for equal representation.

nodes.label: Vidhan Sabha (State Legislative Assembly)
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: State-level legislative body. Members called MLAs, elected from assembly constituencies. Term of 5 years. Chief Minister and state government responsible to the Vidhan Sabha. Number of seats varies by state.

nodes.label: Electoral Roll (Voters' List)
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Official list of all citizens aged 18+ eligible to vote. Prepared before elections, revised every 5 years. Election Photo Identity Card (EPIC) introduced for voter identification. Ensures universal adult franchise in practice.

nodes.label: First Past the Post System (FPTP)
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Electoral system where the candidate with the most votes in a constituency wins. Used in India, UK, and Canada. A candidate can win without majority of votes. Contrasted with proportional representation used in many European countries.

nodes.label: Election Commission of India
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Independent constitutional body (Article 324) that supervises and conducts elections. Headed by Chief Election Commissioner with fixed tenure, can only be removed like a Supreme Court judge. Prepares voters' list, enforces code of conduct, announces results.

nodes.label: General Election
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Elections held in all constituencies simultaneously after Lok Sabha or Vidhan Sabha completes 5-year term or is dissolved. Distinguished from by-elections held to fill single vacancies caused by death or resignation.

nodes.label: By-Election
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Election held for a single constituency to fill vacancy caused by death, resignation, or disqualification of a member. Unlike general elections which cover all constituencies.

nodes.label: Electronic Voting Machine (EVM)
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Device used for recording votes in Indian elections, replacing paper ballots. Each candidate has a button with name and party symbol. Used to reduce election fraud, booth capturing, and invalid votes. Introduced gradually from 1998.

nodes.label: Challenges to Free and Fair Elections in India
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Money power and muscle power influence elections. Candidates with criminal records contest. Caste and religious appeals used for votes. Despite these challenges, India's elections are fundamentally free and fair - people routinely vote out ruling parties.

nodes.label: Prime Minister of India
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Head of government and real executive authority. Leader of majority party in Lok Sabha. Chairs Cabinet meetings, takes major policy decisions, coordinates ministries, and advises President. PM must retain confidence of Lok Sabha.

nodes.label: Civil Servants (Bureaucracy)
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Permanent government officials who implement ministers' decisions. Remain in office even when governments change. Provide continuity, expertise, and institutional memory. Work under political executive's direction.
